full_judgment: 8. The entire argument based on the alleged lack of competence of Anisul Haque in filing the petition of complaint on behalf of his father Shamsul Haque must be held to be not at all well-founded in law. It is an elementary principle of criminal law that any person having knowledge of any criminal offence may set the law in motion by making a complaint even though he is not personally injured or affected by the offence. This is, however, subject to certain limitation that is or may be provided by or under any law. Under section 190 CrPC a competent Magistrate may take cognisance of any offence, among others, upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute such offence. The section does not provide for any qualification or limitation of a person making the complaint of facts but in the subsequent sections, namely, sections 195, 196, 196A, 198 and 199 limitation has been prescribed for the complainant in respect of certain kinds of offences mentioned therein. The complaint in the present case not being inhibited by any of the aforesaid sections could be filed by anybody—either by Shamsul Haque or his son Anisul Haque. Therefore, all the arguments on the basis of the general power of attorney seem to be much ado about nothing.
